This 19th-century South American conflict was the deadliest interstate struggle in Latin American history, pitting one nation against an allied trio of neighboring countries from 1864 to 1870 — which conflict?
Paraguayan War: Major international war in South America (1864–1870)
A close ally of Robespierre, this French revolutionary chose suicide over arrest when authorities stormed the Hôtel de Ville during the coup of 9–10 Thermidor — who was he?
Born in London to a Ugandan-Indian family, this Conservative MP for Witham served as Home Secretary from 2019 to 2022 before becoming Shadow Foreign Secretary — who is she?
Dubbed 'the greatest living explorer' in 1984, this baronet was the first person to reach both poles by surface travel and later summited Everest at age 65 — who is he?
This British Royal Navy officer reached the South Pole in January 1912, just five weeks after a Norwegian rival — but died with his men on the return journey — who was he?
Robert Falcon Scott: British Antarctic explorer (1868–1912)
The seventh adult man ever to embrace Islam, this military commander led the conquest of a Sasanian capital and founded the garrison city of Kufa — who is he?
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: Muslim general (c. 595 – 674)
A philosopher who held a chair in comparative religion at Calcutta before entering public life, this scholar rose from Vice President to President of India in 1962 — who was he?
Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan: President of India from 1962 to 1967. Radhakrishnan's philosophy was grounded in Advaita Vedanta, reinterpreting this tradition for a contemporary understanding.

Spurned in childhood as an illegitimate son, this early-19th-century monarch transformed his kingdom's army into a formidable fighting force during his reign from 1816 to 1828 — who was this Southern African king?
Shaka: Zulu king from 1816 to 1828. King Shaka was born in the lunar month of uNtulikazi (July) in 1787, in Mthonjaneni, KwaZulu-Natal Province, South Africa.
Stepping up from hostess for her assassinated husband, this Sri Lankan politician became, in 1960, the first woman in the world elected prime minister — who was she?
Sirimavo Bandaranaike: Prime Minister of Sri Lanka (1916–2000)
A British barrister who twice held the post of Home Secretary in 2022, this MP for Fareham made headlines in January 2026 by defecting from the Conservatives to Reform UK — who is she?
The first African ever to lead the World Health Organization, this former Ethiopian health and foreign affairs minister steered the agency through Ebola, COVID-19, and the mpox outbreak — who is he?
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus: Ethiopian public health official (born 1965)
A former financial-services man who started on the Charleston County Council, he became the first African-American senator from the South to be directly elected — which South Carolina Republican?
Tim Scott: American politician and businessman (born 1965)
During the American Civil War, what was the name for the federal government and loyal states that refused to recognize the Confederacy after Lincoln's 1860 election?
Union (American Civil War): US federal government from 1861 to 1865.
This former heavyweight boxer holds a PhD and has served as the mayor of Kyiv since 2014 — who is he?
Vitali Klitschko: Ukrainian politician and boxer (born 1971)
Founded, by legend, by Cerdic and Cynric of the Gewisse, this Anglo-Saxon kingdom in southern Britain lasted from around 519 to 927 — what was it called?
Wessex: Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the south of Great Britain.
Son of Darius the Great and a grandson of Cyrus the Great, this Achaemenid King of Kings is best remembered for his doomed 480 BC invasion of Greece — who?
Xerxes I: King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire from 486 to 465 BC.
Nicknamed the 'Young Marshal' after his father's assassination, this Chinese general arrested Chiang Kai-shek in 1936 to force a united front against Japan — who is he?
Zhang Xueliang: Chinese general and warlord (1901–2001)
Which of these people was born first?
Kitty Oppenheimer (born 1910) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four.
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
C (programming language) (founded 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is an astronomer?
Aristarchus of Samos is an astronomer. According to Ptolemy, Aristarchus observed the summer solstice of 280 BC.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Claude Shannon is a mathematician. Shannon was the first to describe the use of Boolean algebra—essential to all digital electronic circuits—and helped found the field of artificial intelligence.
What is the atomic number of Tantalum?
Tantalum is a chemical element; it has symbol Ta and atomic number 73.
What is the atomic number of Copper?
Copper is a chemical element; it has symbol Cu (from Latin cuprum) and atomic number 29.
In what year was Steve Jobs born?
Steve Jobs: Steven Paul Jobs (February 24, 1955 – October 5, 2011) was an American businessman, inventor, and investor.
In what year was Charles Babbage born?
Charles Babbage (26 December 1791 – 18 October 1871) was an English polymath.
In what year was Al-Khwarizmi born?
Al-Khwarizmi: Few biographical details are known about al-Khwarizmi's life.
In what year did Ratan Tata die?
Ratan Tata: Ratan Naval Tata (28 December 1937 – 9 October 2024) was an Indian industrialist and philanthropist.
In what year did Johannes Gutenberg die?
Johannes Gutenberg: Johannes Gensfleisch zur Laden zum Gutenberg (c. 1393–1406 – 3 February 1468) was a German inventor and craftsman who invented the movable-type printing press.
In what year was Ceres discovered?
Ceres is a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
Azithromycin: Pfizer. It is administered by mouth, into a vein, or as topical treatment for the eye.
In which country is Royal Society?
Royal Society: United Kingdom. Founded on 28 November 1660, it was granted a royal charter by King Charles II and is the oldest continuously existing scientific academy in the world.
Who is credited with discovering Archaeopteryx?
Archaeopteryx: Carl Friedrich Häberlein. Archaeopteryx (lit. 'ancient wing'), sometimes referred to by its German name, "Urvogel " (lit. 'Primeval Bird') is an extinct genus of bird-like dinosaurs.
Who is credited with discovering Oganesson?
Oganesson: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
Who is credited with discovering Cimetidine?
Cimetidine: John Colin Emmett. Cimetidine, sold under the brand name Tagamet among others, is a histamine H2 receptor antagonist that inhibits stomach acid production.
Who is credited with discovering Iridium?
Iridium: Smithson Tennant. Iridium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ir and atomic number 77.
Bred for strength and endurance to haul heavy loads across the snow, this large sled-dog breed shares its arctic heritage with breeds like the Siberian Husky and Samoyed — what breed is it?
Alaskan Malamute is a large breed of dog that was originally bred for its strength and endurance to haul heavy freight as a sled dog.

Having led the explosive growth of the American steel industry, this Scottish-American industrialist gave away almost 90 percent of his fortune — about $350 million — in the final 18 years of his life — who is he?
Andrew Carnegie (November 25, 1835 - August 11, 1919) was a Scottish-American industrialist and philanthropist.
Excavated in Argentina starting in 1989 under paleontologist José Bonaparte, this Late Cretaceous titanosaur weighed as much as 80 tons — which genus of giant sauropod?
Argentinosaurus (meaning "lizard from Argentina") is a genus of giant sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina.
Native to the Mekong and Chao Phraya river basins, this freshwater catfish is marketed in the US as "swai" and in the UK as "river cobbler" — which fish?

Basa (fish) (Pangasius bocourti), as it is commonly referred to, is a species of primarily freshwater-dwelling catfish in the shark-catfish family, Pangasiidae, native to the Mekong and Chao Phraya river basins of Mainland Southeast Asia.
Despite its name, this sub-Saharan snake is actually grey to dark brown — the second-longest venomous snake in the world after the king cobra, commonly reaching 3 meters — name this species?
Black mamba (Dendroaspis polylepis) is a species of highly venomous snake belonging to the family Elapidae.
With a mass roughly 13 to 80 times Jupiter's, these substellar objects glow faintly from deuterium fusion rather than true hydrogen burning — what's the term for them?
Brown dwarf are substellar objects that have more mass than the biggest gas giant planets, but less than the least massive main-sequence stars.
Its name comes from the Latin for "coal," and one of its isotopes decays with a 5,700-year half-life that lets scientists date ancient remains — which element is it?
Carbon (from Latin carbo 'coal') is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.
Along with the bonobo, which great ape of equatorial Africa's forests and savannas is humans' closest living relative, according to DNA and fossil evidence?
Chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes), also simply known as the chimp, is a medium-sized great ape species found in the forests and savannas of equatorial Africa.
This digestive condition refers to swelling or inflammation of the large intestine, and can be acute and short-lived or a long-term, chronic issue — what is it called?
Colitis is swelling or inflammation of the large intestine (colon). It broadly fits into the category of digestive diseases.
These echinoderms come in stalked "sea lily" and free-swimming "feather star" forms, with mouths on their upper surface ringed by feeding arms — what class of marine animal is it?
Crinoid are marine invertebrates that make up the class Crinoidea.

Generally moving particles, energy, or other quantities from regions of higher concentration to lower, this stochastic physical process is driven by a gradient in Gibbs free energy and can occasionally even run 'uphill' via spinodal decomposition — name this process?
Diffusion is the net movement of anything (for example, atoms, ions, molecules, energy) generally from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
Born in North Carolina in 1983, this former NSA contractor leaked classified files exposing global surveillance programs after working for the CIA, Dell, and a defense contractor — name him?

Edward Snowden (born June 21, 1983) is a former United States National Security Agency (NSA) intelligence contractor who leaked classified documents revealing the existence of global surveillance programs.
This flowering plant in the family Erythroxylaceae is one of just two species cultivated for their alkaloid-rich leaves — what is its scientific name?
Erythroxylum coca is a species of flowering plant in the family Erythroxylaceae.
Which evergreen conifer genus has needle-like leaves attached singly to the branch by a circular base, and cones that stand upright like a cedar's rather than hanging down? What is it?
Fir are evergreen coniferous trees belonging to the genus Abies in the family Pinaceae.
Named for a long-nosed, insect-eating African animal, this retired supersonic fighter-bomber pioneered variable-sweep wings and automated terrain-following radar in the 1960s — which aircraft?
General Dynamics F-111 Aardvark is a retired, supersonic, medium-range fighter-bomber.
Also called the woodchuck, this North American rodent is exceptional among its kin: while most marmots live in rocky mountains, this lowland burrower roams the Eastern U.S. into Alaska — what is it?
Groundhog (Marmota monax), also known as the woodchuck, is a rodent of the family Sciuridae, belonging to the group of large ground squirrels known as marmots.
With a soft, uncalcified abdomen left dangerously exposed, this crustacean borrows empty snail shells to survive — over 800 species haul their homes around with them. What are they?
Hermit crab are anomuran decapod crustaceans of the superfamily Paguroidea that have adapted to occupy empty scavenged gastropod shells to protect their fragile abdomens.
A person with this condition is excessively and unduly worried about having a serious illness, alarmed by even the most minor symptom — what is it?

Hypochondriasis is a condition in which a person is excessively and unduly worried about having a serious illness. International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) classifies hypochondriasis as a mental and behavioral disorder.

Native to the tropical Americas but now planted worldwide, this flowering plant genus of 49 species has one member so widely introduced it's considered an environmental weed on five continents — what genus is it?
Jacaranda is a genus of 49 species of flowering plants in the family Bignoniaceae, native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas while cultivated around the world.

An Alberta-raised classical liberal who earned his PhD in clinical psychology at McGill and taught at Harvard before the University of Toronto, this commentator drew huge attention in the late 2010s — who is he?
Jordan Peterson (born 12 June 1962) is a Canadian psychologist, author, and media commentator.
Originally a water-retrieving gun dog from Italy's Po Delta marshes, this breed later became prized for hunting truffles once its wetland habitat was drained — what breed is it?
Lagotto Romagnolo is an Italian breed of dog.
This common, soft, movable, painless growth made of fatty tissue usually forms just under the skin, often on the back, shoulders, or abdomen — name this benign tumor?
Lipoma is a benign tumor made of fat tissue. The first use of the term "lipoma" to describe these tumors was in 1709.

Located partly outside the body and partly within the pelvis, this set of sex organs includes the testicles, which produce sperm to fertilize an egg during conception — which body system is being described?
Male reproductive system consists of a number of sex organs that play a role in the process of human reproduction.
Triggered by falling progesterone, this monthly discharge from the uterine lining signals that pregnancy hasn't occurred and typically first arrives at "menarche" between ages 11 and 13 — what is it?
Menstruation (also known as a period, among other colloquial terms) is the regular discharge of blood and mucosal tissue from the inner lining of the uterus through the vagina.
Named from a Greek word for lead because its ores were once confused with lead ore, this chemical element bears the symbol Mo and atomic number 42 — name the element?
Molybdenum is a chemical element; it has symbol Mo and atomic number 42.

What term, coined in the mid-19th century and often attributed to pathologist Rudolf Virchow, describes the premature death of cells in living tissue due to external injury or infection, as opposed to programmed cell death?
Necrosis (from Ancient Greek (nkrsis) 'death') is a form of cell injury which results in the premature death of cells in living tissue by autolysis.
This insect order includes dragonflies and damselflies, the bulkier ones holding wings out at rest while the slender ones fold theirs along the body — what is it?
Odonata is an order of predatory flying insects that includes the dragonflies and damselflies (as well as the Epiophlebia damsel-dragonflies).
Contrasted with 'normophilic' interests and famously tallied at up to 549 types by Anil Aggrawal, this contested clinical category covers atypical sexual attraction — what's its name?
Paraphilia is an uncommon, intense, and persistent sexual arousal or attraction to anything not sexual by nature, though preference is favored for specific designations.

This cellular process, in which a cell's outer membrane engulfs a large particle to form an internal compartment, is a key immune-system mechanism for clearing pathogens and cellular debris — what is it called?

Phagocytosis (from Ancient Greek (phagein) 'to eat' and (kytos) 'cell') is the process by which a cell uses its plasma membrane to engulf a large particle (0.5 m), giving rise to an internal compartment called the phagosome.
Carrying minor-planet number 134340, this icy Kuiper-belt world has about one-sixth the Moon's mass and got demoted when astronomers rewrote the rules — what is it?
Pluto (minor-planet number 134340) is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Unfolding inside every cell in two acts called transcription and translation, this process turns a gene's DNA into messenger RNA on its way to building enzymes and hormones — what is it?
Protein biosynthesis is a core biological process, occurring inside cells, balancing the loss of cellular proteins (via degradation or export) through the production of fresh proteins.

This bird of prey now breeds only in Europe, though it once also ranged across West Asia and Northwest Africa, with northern populations historically wintering as far as western Africa — what bird is it?
Red kite (Milvus milvus) is a bird of prey in the family Accipitridae, which also includes many other diurnal raptors such as eagles, buzzards, and harriers.
This root vegetable — a hybrid of cabbage and a related turnip-like plant — goes by different names in North America and Britain, and is often confused for a big turnip. What is it?
Rutabaga (North American English) or swede (British English and some Commonwealth English) is a root vegetable, a form of Brassica napus (which also includes rapeseed).
This interdisciplinary field studies signs and sign systems, breaking down into branches examining the formal relations between signs, their meanings, and their users — what's the field called?
Semiotics is the study of signs. It is an interdisciplinary field that examines what signs are, how they form sign systems, and how individuals use them to communicate meaning.
A white crystalline compound most important industrially as a nitrite salt, and probably best known as a food additive in processed meats. What is it?
Sodium nitrite is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula NaNO2.

This alkaline earth metal, symbol Sr and atomic number 38, shares chemical properties with its periodic-table neighbors calcium and barium, and is mostly mined from the minerals celestine and strontianite — what element is it?
Strontium is a chemical element; it has symbol Sr and atomic number 38. The metal forms a dark oxide layer when it is exposed to air.
Named for a U.S. state where its discovery research was based, this synthetic element (symbol Ts) holds the second-highest atomic number of all and was the most recently discovered — what is it?
Tennessine is a synthetic element; it has symbol Ts and atomic number 117.
Divided into the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis, this core section of the body is where the head, neck, and all four limbs attach — which body part?
Torso is the central part, or the core, of the body of many animals (including human beings), from which the head, neck, limbs, tail and other appendages extend.
As head of the WWII Office of Scientific Research and Development, this MIT engineer steered nearly all American military R&D, including radar and the early Manhattan Project — who was he?
Vannevar Bush (van-; March 11, 1890 - June 28, 1974) was an American engineer, inventor and science administrator, who during World War II headed the U.S.
This Austrian physicist earned a 1945 Nobel Prize for the exclusion principle and, in 1930, proposed the existence of what would become known as the neutrino — who is he?
Wolfgang Pauli (25 April 1900 - 15 December 1958) was an Austrian theoretical physicist and a pioneer of quantum mechanics.
This bird-of-prey family boasts 256 species including eagles, hawks, kites, and harriers, though the osprey and secretary bird are classified separately — which family is it?
Accipitridae: Family of birds of prey. The Accipitridae have a cosmopolitan distribution, being found on all the world's continents (except Antarctica) and a number of oceanic island groups.
Conceived as a clean-sheet 'extra wide body' answer to Boeing's Dreamliner, this twin-engine jet first lifted off from Toulouse in 2013 on Rolls-Royce Trent power — which airliner is it?
Airbus A350: Large twin-aisle airliner family.
Refined from bauxite and nicknamed alumina, this compound shows up in nature as the mineral corundum — the very stuff of rubies and sapphires. What is it?
Aluminium oxide: Chemical compound. Aluminium oxide (or aluminium(III) oxide) is a chemical compound of aluminium and oxygen with the chemical formula Al2O3.
Named for a modified fin ray it dangles like bait to lure in prey, this order of mostly bottom-dwelling creatures is known for extreme sexual dimorphism between the sexes — what are they called?
Anglerfish: Bony fish with a natural lure.

Once mistaken for bacteria, this domain of single-celled organisms is now known to be the group from which eukaryotes evolved, distinguished by ether-linked cell membranes and a unique whip-like motility structure. What domain is it?
Archaea: Domain of organisms. Traditionally, Archaea included only its prokaryotic members, but has since been found to be paraphyletic, as eukaryotes are known to have evolved from archaea.

Related to the tufted and horned members of its family found in the Pacific, this seabird breeds from Iceland to Newfoundland and dives underwater to catch zooplankton, small fish and crabs — which auk is this?
Atlantic puffin: Species of seabird. The Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica), also known as the common puffin, is a species of seabird in the auk family.

This facial hair — most common among adult men, though it can also appear in women with a condition called hirsutism — has symbolized everything from wisdom and virility to poor hygiene across different cultures — what is it?
Beard: Hair on the chin, lower face and neck.
Patented in 1976 and sold under the brand name Zebeta, this beta-1-selective medication treats high blood pressure and heart failure — what is it?
Bisoprolol: Beta-1 selective adrenenergic blocker medication used to treat cardiovascular diseases.
This white crystalline sodium borate dissolves in water to form a basic solution and finds uses as a pesticide, a soldering flux, and an ingredient in glass and pottery glazes — what mineral is it?
Borax: Boron compound, a salt of boric acid.
Caused by heat, electricity, chemicals, friction, or radiation — and most often the result of scalding at home — what type of skin injury is classified from first- to higher-degree severity?
Burn: Injury to flesh or skin, often caused by excessive heat.
Nicknamed for its heart-shaped seed pods, this mustard-family weed is considered protocarnivorous because its seeds ooze a mucilage that traps nematodes — which species?
Capsella bursa-pastoris: Species of flowering plant in the mustard family.
Which biological process oxidizes nutrients using an electron acceptor such as oxygen to generate ATP, the universal energy currency of life?
Cellular respiration: Process of releasing energy from nutrients using inorganic electron acceptors.

The second-lightest halogen, this yellow-green gas is so reactive it has the highest electron affinity of any element and once fascinated medieval alchemists heating chloride salts — which element is it?
Chlorine: Chemical element with atomic number 17 (Cl)
Striking at the same hour every day for weeks at a time, usually around one eye, this excruciating neurological condition is considered one of the most painful known to medicine — what is it?
Cluster headache: Neurological disorder. The disease is considered among the most painful conditions known to medical science.

Native to Europe and North Africa, this member of the carrot family can grow to 8 feet tall, with hollow stems blotched dark maroon and a distinctly foul smell carried on the wind — which highly poisonous plant is this?
Conium maculatum: Poisonous plant. The plant is herbaceous, with no woody parts, and has a biennial lifecycle.
This practice of secure communication sits at the intersection of math, computer science, and electrical engineering, and underpins e-commerce and chip-based payment cards — what is it called?
Cryptography: Practice and study of secure communication techniques.

Also nicknamed 'the bends,' this diving-related condition happens when dissolved gases form bubbles in body tissue during a too-rapid ascent, often settling painfully in the knees and elbows — what is it called?
Decompression sickness: Disorder caused by dissolved gases forming bubbles in tissues.

He didn't just arrange the known elements — he left gaps and boldly predicted the properties of three undiscovered ones, later vindicated by germanium, gallium, and scandium. Which Russian chemist was he?
Born in 1869 into an old Anglo-Irish scientific family in Dublin, she is considered the world's first woman medical physicist — who was she?
Edith Anne Stoney: Anglo-Irish medical physicist. Edith Anne Stoney (6 January 1869 – 25 June 1938) was an Irish physicist.
This outermost skin layer ranges from about 31 micrometers thick on delicate areas to nearly 600 micrometers on the sole of the foot — what is it?
Epidermis: Outermost of the three layers that make up the skin.

One of the few birds known to pass the mirror test, this highly intelligent corvid found across the northern reaches of Eurasia has a nidopallium proportionally as large as a chimpanzee's brain — which bird is it?
Eurasian magpie: Species of bird. The Eurasian magpie or common magpie (Pica pica) is a resident breeding bird throughout the northern part of the Eurasian continent.
This anaerobic metabolic process, used by humans to preserve and flavor food for some 13,000 years, breaks down sugars to generate ATP when oxygen is scarce — what's it called?
Fermentation: Metabolic redox process producing energy in the absence of oxygen.
This American chemical engineer at Caltech won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for pioneering 'directed evolution' to engineer enzymes — and later joined Alphabet's board — who is it?
Frances Arnold: American chemist and academic (born 1956)
Found on every continent except Antarctica, these lizards are unusual for making vocal chirps and clicks, and most lack eyelids, relying on a transparent membrane instead — what are they?
Gecko: Lizards belonging to the suborder Gekkota.
Occurring in the cytosol, this ten-step metabolic pathway breaks glucose down into pyruvate while generating ATP and NADH — what process is it?
Glycolysis: Series of interconnected biochemical reactions.
After a record 43 years as crown prince, this Swedish monarch approved constitutional reforms stripping the crown of its remaining political powers shortly before his 1973 death. Who was he?
Gustaf VI Adolf: King of Sweden from 1950 to 1973.

This airway symptom — blood or blood-streaked mucus coughed up from the lungs or throat — turns dangerous mainly because of choking rather than blood loss once it passes 300 milliliters. What is it called?

The only birds whose first two neck vertebrae are fused together, these Old World birds have a long down-curved bill sometimes topped with a bony casque, and share an ecological niche with toucans in the Americas — which birds?
Hornbill: Family of birds. The family is omnivorous, feeding on fruit and small animals.
About the size of an almond in humans, this brain structure links the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland — what is it?
Hypothalamus: Area of the brain below the thalamus.
Symbol Fe, atomic number 26, it's the most common element on Earth by mass and forms much of the planet's core — yet smelting it needs furnaces 500°C hotter than copper does. Which metal?
Iron: Chemical element with atomic number 26 (Fe)
With Emmanuelle Charpentier, this Berkeley biochemist proposed in 2012 that CRISPR-Cas9 could edit genomes — work that won them the 2020 Nobel in Chemistry; who is she?
Jennifer Doudna: American biochemist and Nobel laureate (born 1964)
Nicknamed the 'miracle leaf' and 'life plant,' this Madagascar-native succulent sprouts tiny new plantlets right along the edges of its leaves — which species?

Kalanchoe pinnata: Succulent plant native to Madagascar. Kalanchoe pinnata, commonly known as cathedral bells, air plant, life plant, miracle leaf, and love bush, is a succulent plant native to Madagascar.
Named from Greek words for 'hare' and 'form,' this mammalian order splits into rabbits-and-hares on one branch and pikas on the other, totaling around 110 living species — which order?
Also sold as Xylocaine, this amino-amide local anesthetic numbs in minutes and doubles as a treatment for dangerous ventricular heart rhythms — what is it?
Lidocaine: Local anesthetic. Lidocaine, also known as lignocaine and sold under the brand name Xylocaine among others, is a local anesthetic of the amino amide type.

Credited as a 'Father of Cinematography,' this French artist filmed the Roundhay Garden Scene in Leeds in 1888 — then vanished without a trace two years later, and his work never shaped commercial cinema. Who was he?
Louis Le Prince: French motion-picture pioneer (1841–1890s)
Distinguished from living elephants by spirally twisted tusks and a thick coat of fur for cold climates, this extinct genus survived from the late Miocene until roughly 4,000 years ago — what was it?
Mammoth: Extinct genus of mammals. The oldest mammoth representative, Mammuthus subplanifrons, appeared around 6 million years ago during the late Miocene in southern and Eastern Africa.

Marked by small white Koplik spots inside the mouth and a red rash that starts on the face before spreading, this highly contagious, vaccine-preventable disease can bring fevers over 40°C — which disease?
Despite little formal schooling, this self-taught English scientist uncovered the principles behind electromagnetic induction and established the concept of the electromagnetic field — who is he?
Michael Faraday: English chemist and physicist (1791–1867)
Discovered in 1778 by Carl Wilhelm Scheele and boasting the sixth-highest melting point of any element, this metal is mostly used in steel alloys — what is it?
Molybdenum: Chemical element with atomic number 42 (Mo)
Also called flystrike, this parasitic condition occurs when fly larvae infest and feed on the tissue of a living animal — what is it?
An oily alkaloid from nightshade plants like tobacco, it doubles as a potent insect neurotoxin and once served as an insecticide, inspiring the neonicotinoid pesticides — what is it?
Nicotine: Chemical stimulant produced by some plants.
This order of predatory flying insects includes dragonflies and damselflies, whose aquatic larvae are voracious carnivores capable of overpowering small fish and tadpoles — what is it called?
Odonata: Order of insects that includes the dragonflies and damselflies. The adults are superb aerial hunters and their legs are specialised for catching prey in flight.
Sold under the brand name Anavar, this synthetic anabolic steroid helps burn victims and Turner syndrome patients gain weight — what is it?
Oxandrolone: Androgen and anabolic steroid. It was sold under the brand names Oxandrin and Anavar, among others.
This Stanford biologist became famous — and controversial — for his 1968 book warning that runaway population growth would bring famine and resource depletion. Who was he?
First extracted from coal tar and now made from petroleum, this mildly acidic compound is a key precursor to Bakelite and nylon — what is it?
Injected by a mosquito's bite and multiplying first in the liver before invading red blood cells, this parasite genus is the cause of malaria — what is it?
Plasmodium: Genus of parasitic protists that can cause malaria.
Originating in Spain's Canary Islands, this large mastiff-type breed was historically used for guarding, herding sheep and cattle, and — legally until 1936 — dog fighting. Which breed?
Presa Canario: Spanish breed of dog. It originates in the Spanish autonomous community of the Canary Islands, and is found mostly in the islands of Gran Canaria and Tenerife.
This white-yellow-brown fluid forms at sites of infection, and when trapped in an enclosed tissue space, it creates what's known as an abscess — what is it called?
Pus: Fluid produced by inflammatory infection.
Named for the way light stretches toward longer wavelengths, this phenomenon comes in Doppler, gravitational, and cosmological forms and is measured by the value z — what is it?
Redshift: Change in wavelength of light.
This British economist, who won the 1991 Nobel and spent decades at the University of Chicago Law School, urged the field to study real-world wealth creation in Adam Smith's spirit — who was he?
Ronald Coase: British economist and Nobel laureate (1910–2013)
First known as a portrait painter, this American inventor helped develop a single-wire telegraph system and lent his name to the dot-and-dash code introduced in 1837 — who is he?
Samuel Morse: American inventor and painter (1791–1872)
Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, this term for a lucky accidental discovery describes how penicillin, Post-it Notes, and the microwave oven all came about — what is it?

Named in 1842 from Brazilian fossils and often called a saber-toothed tiger despite no close kinship to true tigers, this genus of prehistoric predator roamed the Americas until the early Holocene — which animal?
